items.title: [Nautilus] How Multiple Births Can Accelerate A Mother’s Biological Age
items.content_html:
As any mom can tell you, having a baby takes a big toll. Growing an entire new human being inside your body demands a lot of resources, energy, and time and it can lead to dramatic physiological changes. There’s some evidence that child-bearing benefits longevity, but pregnancy can accelerate biological aging as well. Now, a new review is trying to resolve this tension in the literature.   

Two geneticists from Harvard Medical School surveyed data gathered from studies that measured the biological age of women using a variety of methods, including wearable devices, blood tests and epigenetic clocks, and brain imaging. They found that pregnancy seems to speed up the biological clock, but it slows back down postpartum.  

Read more: “Pregnancy Changes Perception of Odors and Tastes”

items.title: [ArchDaily] Scaffolding as Interior Architecture: The Longevity of Temporary Structures
items.content_html: Scaffolding is perhaps one of architecture's most familiar temporary structures. It accompanies buildings through construction, maintenance, and renovation, only to disappear once its work is complete. Yet its apparent impermanence conceals a different kind of longevity. Scaffolding systems are designed to be assembled, dismantled, transported, and reused, with standardized components robust enough to withstand repeated handling and changing site conditions. Their temporary character lies less in the material itself than in the duration of each assembly.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
items.content_html:
🎨 🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

items.title: [Nautilus] Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 ✏️

With the advent of e-cigarettes, millions of smokers gained a way to get their nicotine fix without many of the negative health effects of lighting tobacco on fire. Of course, because the technology is relatively new, there’s plenty we don’t know about any other adverse long-term effects. That’s one reason it’s particularly troubling that young people have adopted vaping, too. Now the latest data on youth vaping trends is out, and it’s showing some interesting gender differences. 

In a letter published today in JAMA Pediatrics, a team of researchers from the Medical University of South Carolina reports that vaping is on the rise among girls. It’s a bit puzzling. For decades, the reverse was true—more men and boys indulged in nicotine products than women. But according to data from the youth cohort for the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study, girls have been more likely to vape than boys since 2021, with a wider gap in older teens.

Read more: “How Nicotine Disrupts the “Lung-Brain Axis”—And Could Lead to Dementia”

The post Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys appeared first on Nautilus.
